name: Grace Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy dry goods for a food-service distributor out on Harbour Road. Rice, cooking oil, flour, tinned tomatoes, all the boring stuff that restaurants and school kitchens go through by the pallet. Most mornings I'm on the phone to suppliers before eight, checking what's landed and what's late, then I update my spreadsheet by hand because I trust it more than the system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the suppliers. I've got a man at the oil mill who's been selling to us for twenty years and he tells me when prices are about to jump, which no screen will ever do. What wears me out is the price chasing: every week my manager wants a lower number, and I'm the one who has to ring people I like and squeeze them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the world I'd like. Nobody at work has shown me anything AI does that I can't already do with a phone and a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. At lunch I'd tell Priya in accounts that all the noise about AI was a sales pitch, and that buying still comes down to knowing your suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not totally. The company already pushed a new ordering system on us last year and they'd keep using even small AI features as a reason to squeeze the team. My job's fine, but my pay hasn't moved in two years while my rent has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep doing what I do. I'd keep putting a little into savings each month, maybe a hundred, because I've only got about three months put by. And I'd go to the next union meeting, because pay is the real fight here, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a low hum of worry about money. It's the rent letter I think about, not the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent. What's the pressure there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our landlord put the rent up eight percent this spring, and Joel, my partner, is a nurse, so neither of us is on big money. We're fine month to month but we're not getting ahead. A plateau doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two order clerks who key in the invoices. Even boring AI can read an invoice, so if anything gets automated in a plateau, those clerk jobs are the first to go. I'd want the union to make sure those clerks get moved, not dropped.

say: The AI talk was **mostly a sales pitch**, and buying still runs on relationships.
Pay is the **real fight** at our warehouse, not robots.
think: I'm **relieved**, but management would still use small AI features to **squeeze the team**.
My **pay has stalled** for two years while the rent keeps climbing.
do: Keep running supplier calls and my **own spreadsheet** exactly as now.
Put about **100 a month** into savings to stretch a three-month cushion.
Go to the next **union meeting** to push on pay.
feel: A low **worry about money**, driven by the rent rather than the software.
S0.quote: Even boring AI can read an invoice, so if anything gets automated in a plateau, those clerk jobs are the first to go.
fieldNote: Grace dismisses AI quickly but turns straight to **pay and rent**, which are her real pressures.
Her concern for the **order clerks** shows her union instincts even when her own job feels safe.
She trusts her **hand-kept spreadsheet** over the company system, a sign of how she meets change.

steps.text: Keep calling suppliers each morning and updating the spreadsheet by hand
Put about 100 a month into the savings account
Raise pay and clerk jobs at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to home. Buying is right there in the list, isn't it? Writing, checking, planning, buying. That's literally my job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on this before it's rolled out, not after. I'd post something about how companies should have to agree changes with staff, like they do in some countries with works councils, which are staff committees that get a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the slower ones to adjust, and that scares me. The younger buyer, Sam, already plays with chatbots to write supplier emails. If they cut from four buyers to two, I'm not confident I'm one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement on retraining before any new buying software comes in. I'd start cutting back, cancel the gym and the streaming, and try to get to five months of savings by next autumn. And I'd look at jobs in public sector purchasing, the councils and hospitals, because they move slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, honestly. I don't like feeling like I'm about to be left behind by something I chose not to touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fight for retraining, but also that you don't use AI. Would you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. I'd do the course if the company paid and it was in work time, but I won't spend my evenings on it for their benefit. If it's their tool, it's their training bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joel his job is safer than mine for once, which is a funny thing to say to a nurse on night shifts. Then we'd sit down with the bills and see what goes. Probably the holiday we'd planned for June.

say: Companies should need **staff agreement** before rolling out buying software.
Workers deserve a say through something like **works councils**.
think: Buying is **literally my job description** on that list.
If they cut **four buyers to two**, I'm not sure I'd be one of them.
do: Push the union for a **written retraining deal** before new software arrives.
Cancel the **gym and streaming** to reach five months of savings by autumn.
Look at **public sector purchasing** jobs at councils and hospitals.
feel: Some **regret** about avoiding the tools so long.
S1.quote: If they cut from four buyers to two, I'm not confident I'm one of the two.
fieldNote: Grace sees her own role in the card and the **public-private gap** opens: policy talk outside, fear inside.
She'll train only if the **employer pays**, a principled line that may also slow her down.
Public sector buying appeals because it **moves slower**, not because she wants the work.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a written retraining deal before new software
Cancel the gym and streaming and drop the June holiday
Apply for purchasing jobs at the council and the hospital trust

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease is even up. I don't know what to do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this can't be left to the market. Governments would need to step in with some kind of income guarantee, and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone by 2028, plain and simple. My work is nearly all phone calls, spreadsheets and negotiating, and none of that needs a robot. The only bit of me that's hands-on is walking the warehouse to check pallets, and that's maybe an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent, food and bills from the first month. I'd look hard at something hands-on, maybe the warehouse floor or a trade, because the card says robots come three years later, so that buys time. And I'd join whatever campaign group is pushing for a basic income, which is a flat payment everyone gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor tilting. Joel's job might hold but mine wouldn't, and we'd be living on one income in a city we can barely afford on two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of hands-on work before robots. Is that a real plan for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a plan, it's a lifeboat. I'd rather drive a forklift on Harbour Road for three years than sit waiting, but then the robots come for that too. At least it would get us to 2031 and give me time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, I suppose, though I hate that. Rent is sacred because we can't lose the flat. Three months of savings disappears very fast when it's covering half the rent.

say: This can't be **left to the market**; governments must guarantee incomes.
I'd sign every **petition** for a basic income.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**; it's almost all calls and spreadsheets.
Only about **an hour a week** of my work is hands-on.
do: Cut spending to **rent, food and bills** from month one.
Move into **warehouse or trade work** to use the three-year robot gap.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor tilting under me.
**Afraid** of living on Joel's single income in a costly city.
S2.quote: I'd rather drive a forklift on Harbour Road for three years than sit waiting, but then the robots come for that too.
fieldNote: Grace reads her job as **pure thinking work**, so the fast card lands with full force.
The robot delay becomes a **lifeboat**, not a career: she'd take hands-on work just to buy time.
Her answer to fear is **collective and political**, consistent with her views.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Apply for forklift or warehouse floor shifts on Harbour Road
Join a campaign group pushing for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but it's still not long. I'd be thirty-two when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years and no excuse to waste them. At work I'd be pushing the union to negotiate now, while the company still needs us to run the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of my job, just later. I don't think I'd suddenly become an AI person; I'm not built like that. But I could get a qualification in something people need face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder for the first two years, aiming for six months put by. I'd look into an evening course, maybe health and safety or something in logistics on the ground side, since the hands-on bits get an extra three years. And I'd talk to Joel about whether we hold off on trying for a baby until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less panic than the two-year one, more of a slow dread. Like knowing an exam's coming that you can't revise for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not an AI person. Would you try any of the tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, if the job made me. But I'd rather spend my energy on a skill a machine can't do yet than get good at feeding the machine that replaces me. Maybe that's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend thinking of becoming a buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend thinking about buying as a career to pick something with their hands instead. Buying used to be a safe office job with a decent ladder. In this picture the ladder's gone.

say: We have **a few years** and no excuse to waste them.
The union should **negotiate now**, while the company still needs us.
think: It's still the **end of my job**, just later.
I won't become an **AI person**, but I could learn a face-to-face skill.
do: Save toward **six months** of expenses over two years.
Take an **evening course** in health and safety or ground-side logistics.
Talk with Joel about **holding off** on a baby.
feel: A slow **dread**, like an exam you can't revise for.
S3.quote: Buying used to be a safe office job with a decent ladder. In this picture the ladder's gone.
fieldNote: The extra time eases her **panic** but not her expectation of losing the job.
She'd retrain away from screens rather than **learn AI**, a stubbornness she names herself.
The question of a **baby** shows the scenario reaching into family plans.

steps.text: Save toward six months of expenses within two years
Enrol in an evening health and safety course
Decide with Joel whether to wait before trying for a baby
Press the union to open talks on job security now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can almost picture. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can get it right, if we push. Proper public retraining, rules on how fast firms can replace people, all of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably leave buying within five or six years anyway. I'd want to be somewhere with people in front of me. I keep thinking about teaching, or running a canteen kitchen, because I know food supply inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep my job and keep saving, nothing dramatic. I'd start a part-time catering management course in the second year. And I'd stay active in the union, because ten years is time enough to win real protections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. It's like seeing weather coming across the sea. You've got time to get the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you hate changing. Is ten years enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is about the amount of time I need to change, honestly. Two years would break me. Ten lets me do it at my own pace, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. A course and a pay cut while I retrain would eat our savings. If the government paid for retraining like it pays for nurses' training, I'd be first in line.

say: This is the version where we can **get it right** if we push.
We need **public retraining** and rules on how fast firms replace people.
think: I'd probably **leave buying** within five or six years anyway.
I could run a **canteen kitchen**, since I know food supply inside out.
do: Keep **my job** and keep **saving** through the first year.
Start a part-time **catering management** course in year two.
Stay active in the **union** to win protections.
feel: **Uneasy** but steadier than the faster pictures.
Some **hope** that change can happen at my own pace.
S4.quote: Ten years is about the amount of time I need to change, honestly. Two years would break me.
fieldNote: Grace still expects to **lose the buying job**, so anxiety stays, but she has a path.
Her plan moves toward **food and people**, building on what she already knows.
Cost of retraining is the **real barrier**; she wants public funding like nurses get.

steps.text: Keep the buying job and keep saving monthly
Start a part-time catering management course in year two
Stay active in the union to push for job protections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question. Two years isn't long enough for someone like me who's slow to change, and my job is all thinking work. What would help is the government paying for retraining and some income support while I do it, so Joel and I don't lose the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who get squeezed before any of this arrives. Suppliers, clerks, drivers. The pressure on them is already there, and AI just gives management a new excuse.

headlineQuote: I'd rather spend my energy on a skill a machine can't do yet than get good at feeding the machine that replaces me.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old buyer** of dry goods for a food-service distributor, living with Joel, a nurse.
She trusts **supplier relationships** and her own spreadsheet, and has never used AI tools.
Her daily pressure is **pay and rent**, and she looks to the union for answers.
She moves from uneasy in the plateau to **alarmed** in the fast AGI pictures.
With ten years she imagines a **food-service career** working with people instead of screens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job is all thinking work and she's slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and income support so the household keeps the flat.
